messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# James

James was sixty-seven when the pickup truck ran the red light and T-boned his sedan on a Tuesday afternoon in November. He had been driving home from the VA clinic where he worked as a civilian medic three days a week, a job that had kept him anchored since his wife, Patricia, died five years earlier. The impact came from his left. He remembered the sound first—a compression of metal and glass, a noise so complete it seemed to erase everything else. The truck driver had been drinking; James smelled it immediately when the man stumbled out of his cab, a sharp reek of whiskey and beer that cut through the smell of burning rubber and hot engine oil. James, who had spent forty years as a combat medic in the Army, who had stabilized men with catastrophic wounds on three continents, found himself unable to move. His left leg was trapped. When the paramedics arrived, they had to use the Jaws of Life.

The physical injuries healed within months. The fracture in his tibia mended. The lacerations closed. But something had fractured in James that no X-ray could show. By the time he was cleared to return to work, he had stopped driving. At first it was just a caution—his left leg still ached, and the thought of gripping a steering wheel made his chest tight. But as weeks passed, the caution hardened into something else. He could not sit in the passenger seat without his hands beginning to shake. The moment a car approached an intersection, his body would tense. He had come to believe that he could not be trusted behind the wheel, that some failure of judgment or reflex on his part had caused the collision, though the police report clearly stated he had the green light. The thought made no logical sense to him, yet it persisted with the weight of absolute truth. He was a weak person—not physically, but in some deeper way. A strong person would have seen it coming. A strong person would have reacted differently.

He began taking the bus to the VA clinic, a forty-minute journey each way. His supervisor, Dr. Reeves, asked him once if everything was all right. James said yes, but the question lodged in his mind. He watched his own thoughts constantly now, monitoring them for signs that he was losing coherence, that the trauma was fracturing his mind the way it had fractured his body. Whenever he caught himself thinking about the crash, he would forcibly redirect his attention—to a patient's chart, to the weather, to anything else. This worked for short stretches, but the thoughts always returned, often accompanied by the sound of the impact, a deep metallic crunch that played in his head as if a speaker were embedded in his skull.

The worst part was that he could not explain any of this to anyone. When Dr. Reeves asked again, more directly, James opened his mouth to describe what had happened and found that the narrative fragmented. He could see the truck approaching, could smell the alcohol, but when he tried to string these moments into a coherent account, the thread snapped. The memory felt borrowed, as though he were recounting something that had happened to another man, not to himself. This terrified him more than the physical panic did. The fear that he was losing his grip on reality.

At home in the evenings, James would startle at ordinary sounds—the refrigerator humming, a car door closing on the street outside, the neighbor's dog barking. His body would jolt, his heart would race, and it would take minutes for him to settle. He had stopped going to the grocery store because the smell of burnt meat at the deli counter triggered a cascade of physical reactions that left him shaking in the parking lot. The smell of alcohol—anywhere, anytime—sent a spike of adrenaline through his chest.

It was his daughter, calling from Portland, who finally said the words he needed to hear: that he should talk to someone. That what he was experiencing was not weakness, not insanity, but something that could be addressed. At sixty-seven, James had survived wars, had held dying men's hands, had built a life after loss. Yet he could not cross the threshold of his own front door without fear. He called the VA and asked for a referral to mental health. He was terrified of what the answer might be, but he was more terrified of continuing as he was—trapped in a car that no longer moved, a man who could not trust himself, a medic who could no longer heal.
